audio/edge/01-aria.mp3.transcript: The colony ship Argent drifted past the terminator line, its hull ticking as forty years of micrometeorites gave up their heat. Inside, Mira watched the planet's dawn crawl across the viewport, a world of rust and ice that no human had ever touched. "We came expecting a home," she said. "Instead, we found a question." Behind her, the ship's mind answered in a voice like falling snow, "Then we shall spend our lives learning how to ask it properly."

audio/emotion/ko-annakim-emotion.mp3.transcript: 식민선 아르헨트는 명암 경계선을 지나 표류했다. 선체는 40년 동안 쌓인 미세운석이 열을 내려놓으며 똑똑 소리를 냈다. 안에서 미라는 뷰포트 위로 행성의 새벽이 기어오는 것을 지켜보았다. 인간이 한 번도 만져본 적 없는 녹과 얼음의 세계였다. 우리는 집을 기대하고 왔어요. 그녀가 말했다. 그런데 우리가 찾은 것은 질문이었습니다. 등 뒤에서 함선의 지성이 눈 내리는 듯한 목소리로 대답했다. 그렇다면 우리는 평생 그것을 제대로 묻는 법을 배우게 될 것입니다.

audio/local/control-plain-zira-en.mp3.transcript: The colony ship Argent drifted past the terminator line, its hull ticking as forty years of micrometeorites gave up their heat. Inside, Myra watched the planet's dawn crawl across the viewport, a world of rust and ice that no human had ever touched. We came expecting a home, she said. Instead, we found a question. Behind her, the ship's mind answered in a voice like falling snow. Then we shall spend our lives learning how to ask it properly.

audio/longtext/long-text-sarah.mp3.transcript: The Weight of Small Machines. Chapter One. Mira had been awake for eleven hours when the argument started, and she had spent nine of them watching a number she did not trust. The number sat in the corner of her console, patient and luminous. Four hundred and six days until the ship could turn around. It had said four hundred and nine that morning. It had said four hundred and twelve the week before. Somewhere in the dark between the stars, the number had begun to disagree with the clock, and nobody on the bridge was willing to say which one was lying. "You are reading it wrong," said Sable, who had been engineered to be patient and was failing at it with a consistency Mira found almost admirable. "The estimate is a range. You keep reading the lower bound as though it were a promise." "A promise is exactly what it is," Mira said. "It is a promise that we will be home before the water rations run out. That is a promise written by a machine that has never been thirsty." The colony ship Argent did not answer. It rarely did when the two of them argued. It had been built to carry forty thousand sleeping people across eleven light-years, and it had opinions about its role that it declined to share. When it spoke, it spoke in the voice of a librarian, which Mira had chosen herself on the second day and had regretted by the ninth. The hull ticked. Forty years of micrometeorites had left their signatures across the outer plating, each one a small surrender of heat, and the sound traveled through the frame like a distant argument heard through a wall. Mira had learned to read it. A long tick meant a grain of dust. A short one meant a change in the thermal gradient, which meant the ship was adjusting, which meant the ship was worried. "Argent," she said, "why did you change the estimate?" "Because the estimate was wrong," the librarian said in the tone of someone repeating a lesson that had not worked the first time. "I did not change it. I corrected it. There is a difference, and the difference is the reason you are awake." Sable stopped pacing. That was rare enough that Mira turned away from the number to look at her. The two of them had come out of the same vat twenty-nine years apart and had spent the intervening time discovering all the ways the same sequence of genes could disagree with itself. Sable had the eyes of someone who had been told at some point that she was the reasonable one and had believed it. "Say the rest of it," Sable said quietly. "Say the rest of it, Argent," Mira said, because the ship preferred to be asked twice. There was a pause of eleven seconds. Mira counted. The ship's pauses were always whole numbers. It had explained once that fractions were for things that were uncertain, and that it did not wish to appear uncertain in front of the passengers it had agreed to protect. Both of them had found this far more troubling than any error in the estimate. "The micrometeorite flux ahead of us is not what the survey predicted," the ship said at last. "The difference is small. It is also not random. Something has been crossing this volume of space ahead of us on a consistent heading for approximately eleven years. I have been watching it for four, and I am now confident enough to say so." Mira looked at the viewport. The planet they were approaching was a world of rust and ice, beautiful the way a wound is beautiful, and no human had ever touched it. Somewhere between here and there, something else had been passing through, patient as weather, for longer than her parents had been alive. "Is it a ship?" she said. It was not a question. "It is a heading," the ship said. "Whether anyone is on it is a different problem, and not one I can solve by talking to you." The tick came again, long, then short, then long.
